current_paragraph: The Central Bank of The Bahamas issues the Bahamian dollar, which as of December 2025 is held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. The Bahamas scores 28 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed. Its weak point is secrecy: Bahamian law makes it hard to see who owns money there, scoring 75.4 of 100 for financial secrecy, ranked 32 of 141. No government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Two career moves are recorded, neither of them an accusation. T. Baswell Donaldson, who had run the Bahamas Monetary Authority from 1968, was appointed the bank's first governor on 1 June 1974 and served until May 1980; afterwards he chaired the commercial bank Commonwealth Bank, whose ownership is not stated, as well as the Securities Commission, and was ambassador to the United States. James H. Smith was governor from 1987 to 1997 and chairs CFAL, a Nassau investment management and advisory firm that describes itself as the investment arm of Colina Holdings Ltd; he was also a senator and minister of state in the Ministry of Finance from 2002 to 2007. Its board and its exchange rate policy are in the finance minister's hands by statute. Under the Central Bank of The Bahamas Act 2020, the Governor, both Deputy Governors and six other directors are appointed by the Governor-General on the Minister's advice after consulting the Board, and a director or Deputy Governor is removed the same way; section 5(1)(f) makes the bank advise the Minister on exchange rate policy and implement the policy the Minister determines. Giesecke+Devrient printed the bank's new 1-dollar note, introduced on 3 February 2025. The Independent Auditors' Report in the bank's 2011 annual report carries two signature blocks, Deloitte & Touche and BDO, each signed as Chartered Accountants at Nassau on 16 April 2012; later reports print that page as a scanned image.

2020-07-27 · statutory arrangement letting the government direct the bank. The Central Bank of The Bahamas Act, 2020 (Act No. 24 of 2020), published in the Extraordinary Official Gazette of 27 July 2020, leaves the whole of the bank's board in the finance minister's gift and makes the bank implement exchange rate policy the minister sets. Paragraph 2(1) of the Schedule says the Governor, the two Deputy Governors and six other directors are all appointed by the Governor-General on the advice of the Minister after consultation with the Board, and paragraph 4(3) says a decision to remove a director or Deputy Governor is made by the Governor-General on the advice of the Minister after consultation with the Board. Section 5(1)(f) says the bank's functions include advising the Minister on the exchange rate policy and implementing the exchange rate policy determined by the Minister. The Central Bank of The Bahamas (Amendment) Act, 2023 does not amend section 5 or paragraphs 2 and 4 of the Schedule. This is a standing arrangement with no end date. current_paragraph: The Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder, pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 95% of the 194 places scored. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts with plants in Malta and Sweden and a supplier to more than 50 central banks, was contracted to print the new banknotes, with the Royal Canadian Mint making the coins. The bank's supervisory board came under pressure in May 2017. A report published on 26 May 2017 said the board had voted three to two to extend a managing director's term, short of the supermajority required, and that the finance minister, Richard Gibson, had written to the board members Robert Pietersz, Tom Kok, Miriela Carolina, Vance Williams and Hubert Lopez asking them to work on a solution; it quotes him saying that if a solution could not be found there would be no other choice but dismissal of the board, without naming who would carry it out. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a 1.5 million dollar payment in 2015 from the Venezuelan company Enpiso, which prosecutors linked to Girobank takeover talks. One career move is documented: Bob Traa became president with effect from 13 June 2019, after working for the International Monetary Fund for over 34 years, and no private employer is named. That was a temporary appointment by the Supervisory Board, pending official appointment by Curacao and Sint Maarten.

One case is recorded, and it ended in acquittal: in the Khalifa Bank case the Blida criminal court sentenced former governor Abdelwahab Keramane in absentia to 20 years in prison in 2007, and on 7 June 2022 the same court acquitted him. On Monday 23 May 2022 Algeria's president Abdelmadjid Tebboune ended the duties of Rostom Fadhli as governor of the Bank of Algeria, with a statement from the presidency citing article 91 paragraph 7 and article 92 paragraph 7 of the constitution and giving no official reason; Fadhli had been appointed in June 2020 and had been expected to overhaul the 1990 money and credit law, a project that was not completed, and Salah Eddine Taleb, until then secretary of the Money and Credit Council, replaced him. Who checks its books is a state body rather than a firm, and the arrangement sits close to having no outside auditor at all. Under the money and credit law of 21 June 2023, a Censorat of two full-time censeurs, appointed by presidential decree and required to have central bank accounting expertise, verifies the end-of-year accounts, reports to the bank's board and sends a report to the Minister of Finance within four months of the year end. The censeurs are put there by the head of state rather than chosen by the bank, and they answer to a minister; but the Censorat is created by the bank's own charter law and its members sit in its board sessions, which is why this is recorded with the doubt attached. No private firm is named anywhere in the law for the bank's own accounts.

current_paragraph: Lesotho issues the loti, and the South African rand circulates alongside it. The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho, replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and then by a Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined; member currencies are pegged to the rand at par and are legal tender only in the country that issues them, Lesotho must back what it issues fully with rand assets, and South Africa pays it an imputed return on rand circulating there as legal tender. All five of its current notes, introduced on 23 December 2021, are printed by De La Rue. In February 2024 three South Africans appeared in the Ficksburg Magistrates Court on fraud and money laundering charges over 57 million rand said to have been stolen from the Central Bank of Lesotho. The Hawks, a South African police unit, said Lesotho officials intercepted vouchers meant for service providers and diverted the payments to co-conspirators in South Africa, and that some officials were already before court in Lesotho. The charges are unproven. One career move is recorded, and it is not an accusation: Mr. O. 'Nete, a non-executive director on the bank's board, came from Standard Bank of Lesotho, where he was Senior Finance Manager, Finance Manager and Senior Manager Personal Credit, and earlier from Stanlib, where he was Tax Manager, with no dates given; Standard Bank Group's own structure page lists Standard Lesotho Bank Limited at 80 per cent among its holdings as at 30 June 2026, so that employer is majority owned by the Johannesburg-listed group rather than by the state. Its 2023 accounts were audited by Moteane, Quashie & Associates with SizweNtsalubaGobodo Grant Thornton. Lesotho scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and corruption and secrecy around the bank is its weakest side, at 60. At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, the parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. Its chairperson, 'Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures in the report do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the consolidated accounts, a difference of M3.09 billion, which a quotation in the same piece also gives. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget for the audit by 30 June so it could go into the supplementary budget; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for one. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes for the state.

At a hearing on Monday 8 June 2026, at which the Auditor General presented consolidated financial statements for 31 March 2023 and 2024, Lesotho's parliamentary Public Accounts Committee called for a forensic audit of the Central Bank of Lesotho to trace missing public money. The committee's chairperson, 'Machabana Lemphane-Letsie, said the bank must undergo a forensic audit and say who the money had been paid to. The figures the report gives do not agree with each other: its headline puts the gap at M3.9 billion, while the statements it describes show government cash of M5.91 billion at 31 March 2024 against M2.82 billion in the Consolidated Financial Statements, a difference of M3.09 billion, and a quotation in the same piece also gives M3.09 billion. The committee resolved that the Auditor General's office submit a budget proposal for the forensic audit by 30 June so it could go into the supplementary budget; that office said it has neither the expertise nor any budget allocated for such an audit. The bank resisted, citing its own 2000 Act, which provides for an external auditor and limits the Auditor General to auditing currency balances rather than government payments the bank makes on the state's behalf. Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

Common Monetary Area (common monetary area)

The Rand Monetary Area agreement was signed in December 1974 by South Africa, Swaziland and Lesotho; it was replaced by the Common Monetary Area in July 1986 and by the Multilateral Monetary Agreement in February 1992, when Namibia formally joined.
Member currencies have been pegged to the rand at par since their introduction; they are legal tender only in the issuing country.
Lesotho and Namibia must fully back their currency issues with rand assets; Eswatini does not face this requirement.
The rand has not been de jure legal tender in Eswatini since 1986.
South Africa makes compensatory payments representing an imputed return on rand circulating as legal tender in Lesotho and Namibia; Eswatini has received none since 1986.

current_paragraph: The National Bank of Tajikistan issues the somoni, which it keeps within a band of 2 per cent or less against the US dollar. The Law on the National Bank of Tajikistan, No. 722 of 28 June 2011, signed by President Emomali Rahmon, puts every seat on the bank's Board in the President's hands. Article 74(4) has the Chairman and his deputies appointed and released from office by presidential decree, with the decrees submitted to the lower house of parliament for approval; article 74(3) has the Board's three independent members approved by the President on the Chairman's proposal; and article 74(6) has the President set the salary of the Chairman and his deputies. One case is recorded, as an official finding: in March 2008 the International Monetary Fund's Executive Board found the bank had supplied inaccurate information on the cotton sector, international reserves, net domestic assets and credit policy, reporting reserves of about 450 million US dollars when they were roughly a third of that and concealing that reserves were pledged as collateral for cotton loans; Tajikistan was required to repay 47.4 million US dollars. No government pressure was reported from 2010 to 2018. It has one swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency: 3 billion yuan with China, signed on 3 September 2015 to run three years and extendable by agreement, drawn on for 1 million yuan in January 2016; whether it is in force is not known. Its commemorative 100-somoni note, circulated on 30 October 2025, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient of Germany, that note alone and not the regular series. RSM Tajikistan LLC signed the auditor's report on the 2023 statements; the firm holds a licence to audit banks issued by the National Bank itself, so the body being audited also licenses its auditor. Earlier audits were done by Deloitte and by Ernst & Young Ford Rhodes Sidat Hyder. Tajikistan scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed.

current_paragraph: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. Its own law lets the government direct it: under the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan 2010, passed on 2 June 2010 and in force from 22 June 2010, section 149 lets the Royal Government issue such directives to the Authority as it considers necessary in the public interest, after consulting the Governor and reporting them to Parliament. Four of the Board's seven members are appointed by the Government, one of them from the Ministry of Finance, and the Royal Government sets the Governor's salary and the board members' fees. The Governor is appointed by the Druk Gyalpo on the Prime Minister's recommendation and may be removed the same way, but only on a committee finding of permanent incapacity, incapability of carrying out the duties or breach of the code of conduct. The Act repealed the 1982 Royal Monetary Authority Act, and the arrangement is standing, with no end date. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. One career move is recorded, and every post in it is a public one: Dasho Penjore began at the Royal Monetary Authority in 1987, was its Deputy Managing Director from 2003 to 2006, was appointed Chief Chamberlain to the King in 2006, was Chief Executive Officer of the National Pension and Provident Fund of Bhutan, a statutory pension body, and was appointed Governor of the Authority in December 2015. A commemorative 1,000-ngultrum note marking the Fourth King's seventieth birth anniversary was printed by De La Rue, and M/s P.K. Mitra & Company audited the accounts for 2003 and 2004. India opened a swap line, an arrangement to borrow another central bank's currency, of up to 100 million US dollars or its equivalent on 17 March 2016 under the Reserve Bank of India's SAARC framework; its three-year term ran out in March 2019.
